t: Maximum Multiplication Score — Fixed-Length Alignment DP
o: Pick 4 increasing indices in b and maximize a[0]*b[i0] + a[1]*b[i1] + a[2]*b[i2] + a[3]*b[i3]. Since |a| = 4 is a constant, this is an alignment problem: sweep b left to right and decide for each element whether it consumes the next unused element of a. Example 1 aligns 3,2,5,6 with b-values 2,-6,4,2 for 26. With |b| up to 1e5, an O(n^4) enumeration is hopeless, but an O(4n) DP is trivial.
k: Only 4 choices must be matched, so a DP whose state is 'how many of a are already matched' suffices.
Processing b in order and updating the match count downward guarantees each b element is used at most once and indices stay increasing.

a.i: Let dp[k] be the best score using exactly the first k values of a among the b-elements processed so far. Scanning b and relaxing k from 3 down to 0 in place ensures each b element is taken at most once. The answer is dp[3] after the scan.
s: For each x in b, for k = 3 down to 1: dp[k] = max(dp[k], dp[k-1] + a[k]*x).
a.t: O(4n) — one constant-size relaxation per element of b.
a.sp: O(1) — a fixed array of 4 entries.

a.i: Define f(j, k) = best score matching a[k..3] onto b[j..]. At each step either skip b[j] or pair it with a[k]. This is the same recurrence viewed recursively; it needs a raised recursion limit in Python because the skip-chain can be n deep.
s: f(j, 4) = 0; f(j, k) = -inf if not enough elements remain.
a.t: O(4n) — each state (j, k) is computed once with O(1) work.
a.sp: O(4n) — the memo table (plus recursion stack).

w: Prefer the iterative rolling DP: same complexity, no recursion-depth risk. Common pitfalls: updating dp in ascending k order (which lets one b element be reused), and forgetting that all values can be negative so the answer may be negative — initialize with -infinity, not 0. Follow-up: generalize to |a| = m; the same DP is O(mn).
